Imagine the ship that brought you
here sails over the horizon,
and it never comes back.
There are no trees,
no soil, no river,
only a flat strip of white sand
and coral, less than two kilometers
long, in the middle of the Indian Ocean.
Could you last a week?
A month?
In 1761, around sixty Malagasy
men and women were left behind
on exactly this kind of island,
called Tromelin.
Fifteen years later, seven women
and one baby were still alive.
How does anyone survive that long
on a sandbank that offers almost
nothing, and why did the world forget them?
If you look at a map of
the southwestern Indian Ocean,
you will mostly see an endless
expanse of deep blue.
East of Madagascar and north of
Réunion, there is a speck so small
that many maps do not even print its name.
It is a lonely coral island called Tromelin.
It is about seventeen hundred meters
long and seven hundred meters wide,
and its highest point rises only
about seven meters above the waves.
There are no rivers,
no shady groves, and no hills to
shield you from the wind.
It is an open strip of sand,
completely defenseless against the sea.
Before it carried the name Tromelin,
it was simply known as Sand Island,
and that name says it all.
Cyclones sweep across these waters
every year, and nothing on the
island can slow them down.
To understand this story,
we have to travel back to 1761.
A French East India Company ship
named the Utile was sailing across
the Indian Ocean.
Its captain, Jean de La Fargue,
had taken on well over a hundred
enslaved Malagasy men and women
in Madagascar, even though he was
not authorized to trade in people.
They were packed below deck,
bound for the French colony of
Isle de France, known today as Mauritius.
To the men who ran the ship,
the people in the hold were cargo.
Navigating the ocean in the
eighteenth century was a dangerous gamble.
There was no satellite and no radio,
and a small error could put a
ship on a reef.
Charts were inaccurate, and captains
relied on dead reckoning,
an estimate of position from speed
and heading.
On the night of July thirty-first,
1761, the navigators believed they
were in open water,
far from any danger.
They were wrong.
In the darkness lay a ring of
coral reef, and nobody on board
knew it was there.
The Utile ran hard aground.
Waves pounded the hull,
and the ship began to break apart.
The sailors scrambled for the upper
decks and the boats,
while the enslaved people below
were trapped in the dark.
Many of them did not make it out.
Those who did fought through the
churning surf.
When the sun rose the next morning,
the survivors found themselves
standing on a flat, barren sandbank.
More than one hundred and twenty
French crew members, and around
sixty Malagasy men and women,
had made it to shore.
Relief quickly turned to dread.
The island was utterly barren.
There was not a single tree to
give shade from the equatorial sun.
There was no fruit,
no edible roots, and,
most frightening of all,
no stream of fresh water.
How long could anyone last in an
open-air prison made of blinding white sand?
Water was the first challenge.
Without it, death would come within days.
The survivors began to dig into the sand.
At first, the holes filled with seawater.
But a well dug deep enough reached
a layer of water that was slightly
salty, yet drinkable.
On small sand islands,
rain can soak into the ground and
float as a thin layer above the
heavier seawater below.
That is the layer they reached.
That single crude well became their
lifeline, and it kept them alive.
With water secured, the French
crew began planning their escape.
They salvaged timber, sails,
and iron nails from the wreck that
washed ashore.
Within about two months,
they used these scraps to build
a small boat.
They named it the Providence.
The Malagasy survivors helped where
they could, and they,
too, hoped to leave.
But the moment of completion brought
a cruel revelation.
The boat was too small to carry everyone.
Only the French sailors would board.
The Malagasy survivors were told
they had to remain behind.
Can you imagine watching that boat
prepare to launch?
The sailors left them a few
supplies, some tools, and a promise.
On the way, they said,
they would return with a ship.
On the twenty-seventh of September,
1761, one hundred and twenty-two
French sailors pushed off through the surf.
The Malagasy survivors stood on
the beach, watching the sail shrink
until it vanished over the horizon.
The Providence reached Madagascar,
and from there the crew made their
way to Isle de France.
Their first officer, Barthélemy
Castellan du Vernet, begged the
governor to send a vessel for the
people left behind.
But the answer he received was cold.
The Seven Years' War was raging,
and the colony's resources were
stretched thin.
Worse, the governor, Antoine Marie
Desforges-Boucher, was reportedly
furious that the Utile's captain
had broken the rules on trading in people.
The governor refused to send a
ship, and the request was turned
down again and again.
In the years that followed,
the island slipped from the minds
of the colonial authorities.
To understand how anyone survived,
we have to look at what this
island did offer.
There were no edible plants,
but the island was a nesting ground
for seabirds.
Many thousands of them,
mostly sooty terns, laid eggs on the sand.
Sea turtles hauled themselves onto
the beaches at night to lay theirs.
Birds, eggs, turtle meat,
and some fish became the foundation
of the castaways' diet.
Food alone is not enough.
On a sand island,
fire is life.
Without fire, meat cannot be cooked,
warmth cannot be found on cold
nights, and the days stay dark.
Archaeologists later found flint,
fire strikers, and nails from burned
ship timber.
Historians report that the survivors
kept a fire burning for fifteen
years, fed by driftwood and pieces
of the wreck.
We do not know every detail of
how they did it.
But their rescuers found a fire still lit.
A fire on a sand island does
more than cook.
It gives light in the dark,
warmth in the cold wind,
and a signal that people are here.
Perhaps that mattered most to people
who spent every day watching the
sea for a sail.
Think about the dedication that took.
There were no forests to cut for firewood.
Someone had to walk the beaches
every day, collecting whatever
the ocean left behind.
Fifteen years is more than five thousand days.
For centuries, the story of the
castaways survived only in a few
old documents, and many people
doubted how much of it was true.
Then, in 2006, a French team led
by Max Guérout, a former naval
officer and underwater
archaeologist, began to dig on the island.
They returned in 2008,
in 2010, and again in 2013,
when the work lasted forty-five days.
What they found backed up the old
records, and added a great deal more.
The team found something extraordinary.
These people did not just huddle
in the sand.
They built a settlement.
At the highest point of the island,
they raised low, sturdy buildings
from beach sandstone slabs set
upright and topped with coral blocks.
Low walls helped protect them from
the wind that sweeps the island.
Even the food leaves a trace.
In 2013, the team recovered about
eighteen thousand bird bones,
most of them from sooty terns,
along with bones of turtles and fish.
It is a record of how people
ate on an island with nothing else to eat.
The excavations also uncovered
copper bowls and utensils from the wreck.
These were not left to rust.
The survivors hammered the copper
and repaired their cookware again
and again, some pieces as many
as eight times over the years.
In a place with no new materials,
every scrap of metal mattered.
Still, life was an endless struggle.
Sickness and the strain of waiting
slowly reduced their numbers.
In the years before the rescue,
a small group of the castaways
built a craft and sailed away,
hoping to reach land.
They were never heard from again.
By the end, the community that
remained was made up mostly of women.
They kept the well,
gathered food, tended the fire,
and raised a child.
We can only imagine how they
supported one another through grief,
sickness, and the weight of endless waiting.
Imagine standing on that beach
after ten years had passed.
Would you still believe someone
was coming for you?
The horizon was always empty,
a circle of blue meeting blue.
An entire decade of your life,
on a strip of sand you could
walk across in less than half an hour.
Many people would have lost hope.
Yet this community kept living,
and they kept the fire alive.
They had every reason to believe
the world had forgotten them,
because it largely had.
Help did try to come.
Rescue attempts in the 1770s were
turned back by the surf or wrecked
on the reef.
At last, in November of 1776,
fifteen years and four months after
the Utile was lost,
the corvette La Dauphine reached the island.
Its commander was a young naval
officer, Jacques Marie Boudin de Tromelin.
On November twenty-ninth, a boat
finally made it through the surf.
On the white sand,
the sailors found the survivors,
who had been waiting for fifteen
years and four months.
After more than fifteen years,
how many people do you think were left?
Out of about sixty Malagasy men
and women who had stayed behind
in 1761, only seven women remained.
With them was an eight-month-old
baby boy, born on the sandbank.
He knew no other world than crashing
waves, seabird cries, and the women
who kept him alive.
The sailors carried them across
the reef to the corvette.
In Isle de France,
the governor, Maillart, declared them free.
The baby boy was given the name Jacques Moyse.
The island was later named Tromelin
after the officer who rescued them,
and it still bears that name on maps today.
But for many modern historians,
it is not a monument to the officer.
It is a monument to the eight
people who turned a barren sandbank
into a place where life continued.
Their survival was not an accident.
It was a daily act of courage,
ingenuity, and community.
Think back to the questions we
asked at the beginning.
What keeps us going when everything
familiar is taken away?
We often look at the comforts of
modern life, our phones,
our heated rooms, our endless
supplies of food, and assume that
our strength comes from the tools around us.
But Tromelin suggests something deeper.
The ultimate tool for survival
is not technology.
It is our capacity to adapt,
to cooperate, and to hold on to
hope when there is little reason
to hope at all.
The next time you feel stranded
by circumstances you cannot control,
remember the seven women on the sandbank.
Remember the fire that,
according to the historians,
burned for fifteen years through
wind, rain, and cyclone.
Like that small fire carefully
tended on a lonely shore,
hope is a flame best kept alive together.
